# Janavasabha Sutta (DN 18 (PTS DN ii 200))

**ID:** DN 18 (PTS DN ii 200)
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Janavasabha Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** With Janavasabha
**PTS:** DN ii 200
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/dn18
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0102m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Janavasabhasutta* (DN 18) begins at the Brick House in Nādikā with an account of the rebirth destinations of recently deceased disciples, before the narrative turns to a revelation granted to the Buddha by the *yakkha* Janavasabha [SuttaCentral; Norman 1983; Piya Tan 2004]. Janavasabha is revealed to be the former king Bimbisāra of Magadha, now reborn into the retinue of the World Guardian Vaiśravaṇa (Pali: Vessavaṇa) [Goble 2012; Radich 2007]. He reports on an assembly in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three (Tāvatiṁsa), where the gods rejoice that their ranks are swelling with newly reborn disciples of the Buddha, followed by the radiant appearance and Dhamma discourse of Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra [SuttaCentral; Polak 2011; Radich 2007]. Multiple scholars have noted that this text constitutes an elaboration of the Nādikā episode from the *Mahāparinibbānasutta* (DN 16); Kenneth Roy Norman observes that its prominent mythical elements and numerical treatment of doctrine suggest that it is a later insertion into the collection [Norman 1983; Piya Tan 2002; Thomas 1933].

Doctrinally, the discourse contains an important discussion of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), specifying that external contemplation (*bahiddhā*) involves directing awareness to the bodies, feelings, minds, and phenomena of others (*parakāye*, *paravedanā*, *paracitta*, *paradhamma*) after establishing internal concentration [Anālayo 2014; Wen]. It also preserves a standard verse describing how apparitions (*nimmitā*) speak or remain silent in unison with their creator, a passage cited across various non-Theravāda treatises and commentaries [Radich 2007; Tournier et al.]. DharmaNexus records substantial internal text reuse with 188 other Pali texts, sharing the largest blocks of material with the *Mahāgovinda Sutta* (DN 19, over 20,000 characters), the *Iddhipāda Saṁyutta* (SN 51), the *Sotāpatti Saṁyutta* (SN 55), the *Naḷakapāna Sutta* (MN 68), and the *Satipaṭṭhāna Saṁyutta* (SN 47) [DharmaNexus].

Curated parallels include two Chinese translations: Dīrghāgama discourse 4 (*She ni sha jing* 闍尼沙經 in T 1) and the independent *Renxian jing* (人仙經, T 9), both of which are also matched in DharmaNexus alignments [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Tournier et al.]. Sanskrit versions are attested in Turfan manuscript fragments (SHT sutta37) and Dīrghāgama witnesses from Central Asia and Gilgit (*Janarṣabha-* or *Jinayabha-sūtra*), alongside parallels in the *Theragāthā* (Thag 16.9) and canonical citations in Śamathadeva's *Abhidharmakośopāyikā-ṭīkā* [SuttaCentral; Tournier et al.].
